title: Query Rewriting & Agentic RAG
summary: Classic RAG retrieves once on the user's raw query and hopes it's phrased well. Agentic RAG treats retrieval as a tool the agent controls: it rewrites vague or conversational queries into good search queries, expands one question into several sub-queries, and loops — retrieving, reading, and deciding whether it needs more before answering. The agent, not a fixed pipeline, decides when and what to retrieve.

subtopics.title: Raw user queries make poor search queries
subtopics.explanation: Users ask conversationally — 'what about the second one?', 'does it work for us?' — with pronouns, context from earlier turns, and no keywords. Embedded verbatim, these retrieve badly because they lack the terms and specificity that match relevant chunks. Rewriting the query into a standalone, keyword-rich search string is the cheapest agentic-RAG upgrade because it fixes retrieval at the input before any index is touched.
subtopics.example:
history = ["Tell me about the Pro plan.", "Does it include SSO?"]
raw = "does it include SSO?"          # 'it' is unresolved -> bad retrieval

# rewrite into a standalone, searchable query
rewritten = rewrite(history, raw)
print(rewritten)
# 'Does the Pro plan include SSO (single sign-on)?'
# now the embedding carries the entities the index can match

subtopics.title: Rewrite for clarity, expand for coverage
subtopics.explanation: Rewriting resolves references and adds keywords to a single query; expansion goes further by generating several query variants or sub-questions so retrieval covers different phrasings and facets of the need. You run all variants, then merge and dedupe the retrieved chunks. Expansion trades extra retrieval calls for higher recall, which is the right bet when one phrasing of a query reliably misses relevant chunks the others would catch.

subtopics.title: Retrieval as a tool the agent calls
subtopics.explanation: Instead of a fixed retrieve-then-generate pipeline, you expose retrieval as a tool with a schema, and let the agent decide to call it — with a query it composes — as one action in its loop. This puts retrieval on equal footing with other tools, so the model can search, read the observation, and choose to search again with a refined query. Making retrieval a tool is the structural shift that turns static RAG into agentic RAG.

subtopics.title: Multi-step retrieval for compositional questions
subtopics.explanation: Some questions can't be answered by one lookup — 'which plan has SSO, and is it cheaper than a competitor's?' needs a fact retrieved, then a second retrieval informed by the first. An agentic loop retrieves, reads the result, and issues a follow-up query grounded in what it just learned, chaining lookups until it has enough. This iterative retrieve-read-refine is what lets RAG answer multi-hop questions a single-shot retrieval structurally cannot.

subtopics.title: Let the agent decide WHEN to retrieve
subtopics.explanation: Not every turn needs retrieval — a greeting, a follow-up the agent can answer from context, or arithmetic shouldn't trigger a search. Giving the agent the choice (retrieve, or answer directly) avoids wasted lookups and latency, but demands a stopping condition so it doesn't loop forever chasing more context. Deciding when to retrieve, not just what, is what makes agentic RAG efficient rather than a query-amplifier.
subtopics.example:
def maybe_retrieve(agent, question, context):
    plan = agent.plan(question, context)
    if plan.needs_search:                 # only search when it helps
        return vector_store.search(plan.query, k=5)
    return None                           # answer directly, no lookup

# a 'thanks!' or a fact already in context skips retrieval entirely
chunks = maybe_retrieve(agent, "thanks, that's all", context)  # None

foundations.overview: Classic RAG is a fixed pipeline: take the user's query, embed it, retrieve top-k, stuff the chunks in the prompt, generate. It works when the query is already a good search query and one lookup suffices — and fails when it isn't. Agentic RAG replaces the fixed pipeline with an agent that controls retrieval. First, it rewrites the raw query: conversational messages full of pronouns and missing keywords ('does it support that?') are turned into standalone, keyword-rich search strings that actually match relevant chunks. It can expand one query into several sub-queries to cover different phrasings and facets, then merge the results for higher recall. Structurally, retrieval becomes a tool with a schema that the agent calls with a query it composes, on equal footing with other tools. That unlocks multi-step retrieval: the agent searches, reads the observation, and issues a follow-up query grounded in what it just learned, chaining lookups to answer compositional, multi-hop questions. And because retrieval is a choice, the agent decides when to retrieve at all — skipping the lookup for greetings or context it already has — bounded by a stopping condition so it doesn't loop forever. The through-line: the agent, not a static pipeline, owns the retrieval strategy.
foundations.formalDefinition: Agentic RAG models retrieval as an action available to an LLM agent: the agent may transform the query (rewrite/expand), invoke a retrieval tool retrieve(query) -> chunks zero or more times, incorporate each result into its state, and decide at each step whether to retrieve again or answer, subject to a termination bound. Classic RAG is the degenerate case of exactly one retrieval on the unmodified query.
foundations.whyItMatters: Real queries are conversational, ambiguous, and sometimes multi-hop, and a single verbatim retrieval frequently fetches the wrong context or misses a needed second fact. Letting the agent rewrite, expand, and iterate — and skip retrieval when it isn't needed — directly lifts answer quality on exactly the hard queries where fixed-pipeline RAG breaks down.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the difference between a vending machine and a research assistant. Classic RAG is the vending machine: put in the exact query, get one shelf of results, done. Agentic RAG is the assistant: they reword your fuzzy request into good search terms, look several things up, read what came back, go look up a follow-up if needed, and only skip the library entirely when they already know the answer.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Conversational RAG assistants that resolve pronouns against chat history before searching, deep-research agents that decompose a question into sub-queries and chain lookups, and tool-using agents where 'search the docs' sits alongside 'run SQL' and 'call the API' as one action the model chooses.
commonUseCases: Conversational search where queries reference earlier turns
Recall-sensitive queries answered by expansion into sub-queries
Agents that mix retrieval with other tools and skip it when unneeded

commonMisconceptions.myth: Agentic RAG just means retrieving more.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The point is retrieving smarter: rewriting for clarity, expanding for coverage, chaining for multi-hop, and skipping retrieval when it isn't needed. More undirected retrieval adds latency and noise, not quality.

For conversational queries it's often the single biggest retrieval win, because a verbatim pronoun-laden message embeds to a poor vector; a standalone rewrite fixes retrieval at the input for the price of one cheap model call.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An agentic loop can search until it's satisfied.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unbounded iterative retrieval can loop and rack up cost. Agentic RAG needs a step cap and a clear 'enough context' or 'answer now' stopping condition, exactly like any agent loop.

interactiveExamples.title: Agentic retrieval loop with a retrieve-or-answer decision
interactiveExamples.explanation: A bounded loop where a policy stub decides at each step whether to search (with a query it composes) or answer. It chains a second retrieval informed by the first, then answers — the core of multi-step agentic RAG.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does a conversational query like 'does it include SSO?' retrieve poorly if embedded verbatim?
options: It's too long for the embedding model
The pronoun 'it' carries no retrievable entity, so the vector lacks the keywords that match relevant chunks
SSO is not a real term
checkpoints.explanation: The unresolved pronoun means the query vector doesn't encode the actual subject (e.g. 'Pro plan'), so it can't match the right chunks. Rewriting it into a standalone, entity-rich query fixes retrieval at the input.

checkpoints.prompt: What structural change turns classic RAG into agentic RAG?
options: Exposing retrieval as a tool the agent chooses to call (with a query it composes), so it can search, read, and search again
checkpoints.explanation: Making retrieval a tool the agent invokes in its loop — deciding when and what to search — is the structural shift. That enables rewriting, expansion, multi-step retrieval, and skipping retrieval when it isn't needed.

checkpoints.prompt: This agentic-RAG loop can hang in production. What's missing?
checkpoints.code:
def agentic_rag(question, agent):
    notes = []
    while True:                       # keep going until the agent answers
        action = agent.decide(question, notes)
        if action.type == "answer":
            return action.text
        notes.append(search(action.query))
options: There's no step cap or budget, so if the agent never emits 'answer' the loop runs forever and racks up retrieval cost
checkpoints.explanation: An agentic loop needs a stopping condition — a max-step cap plus an 'answer now' fallback. Without one, an agent that keeps deciding to search never terminates, exactly like any unbounded agent loop.

theory.question: What is agentic RAG, and how does it differ from classic RAG?
theory.directAnswer: Classic RAG is a fixed pipeline: embed the user's query, retrieve top-k once, and generate. Agentic RAG makes retrieval a tool the agent controls — it rewrites the raw query into a good standalone search string, can expand it into several sub-queries for coverage, and loops: search, read the result, and decide whether to search again (with a refined query) or answer. The agent, not a static pipeline, decides when and what to retrieve, which lets it handle conversational, ambiguous, and multi-hop questions that one verbatim retrieval can't.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A RAG design where an LLM agent owns the retrieval strategy — query transformation, tool-based retrieval, and iteration — rather than a hard-coded retrieve-then-generate flow.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real queries are conversational and sometimes multi-hop, so a single verbatim retrieval often fetches wrong context or misses a needed second fact; giving the agent control fixes retrieval where the fixed pipeline is brittle.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Retrieval is exposed as a tool with a query parameter; the agent rewrites/expands the query, calls the tool, incorporates the observation, and re-decides each step under a termination bound. Classic RAG is the one-shot special case.

theory.whyImportant: It's the difference between RAG that works only on well-phrased single-lookup questions and RAG that holds up on the messy, compositional queries users actually ask.
theory.realWorldExample: A support assistant rewrites 'does it do that?' against chat history into 'does the Pro plan support SAML SSO?', retrieves, sees it needs pricing too, issues a second query, and then answers both parts.

followUps.question: Does agentic RAG always beat classic RAG?
followUps.answer: No — for well-phrased single-lookup queries it adds latency and cost for little gain. It wins on conversational, ambiguous, or multi-hop queries; you often route only hard queries into the agentic path.

followUps.question: What's the cheapest agentic-RAG improvement?
followUps.answer: Query rewriting: one cheap model call that turns a pronoun-laden message into a standalone, keyword-rich query, often the biggest single retrieval win for conversational systems.

theory.question: What are query rewriting and query expansion, and when do you use each?
theory.directAnswer: Rewriting transforms a single query for clarity — resolving pronouns, adding keywords, making it standalone — so it embeds to something the index can match; it's cheap and used on nearly every conversational query. Expansion generates several query variants or sub-questions and merges their retrieved chunks to cover different phrasings and facets, trading extra retrieval calls for higher recall; you use it when one phrasing reliably misses relevant chunks the others would catch, such as multi-faceted or recall-sensitive queries.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two query-transformation techniques: rewriting (clarify one query) and expansion (diversify into many).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single raw query is often under-specified or captures only one facet of the need; rewriting fixes specificity and expansion fixes coverage.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Rewriting is one model call producing a standalone query used for retrieval; expansion is a model call producing N variants, each retrieved separately, with results merged and deduped before generation.

theory.whyImportant: They target the two distinct ways retrieval-at-the-input fails — vagueness and narrow coverage — and choosing the right one avoids paying expansion's extra retrieval cost when a cheap rewrite would do.
theory.realWorldExample: A cancel-and-refund question is expanded into 'how to cancel', 'refund after cancellation', and 'prorated charges', whose union surfaces chunks no single phrasing retrieved.

followUps.question: How do you merge expanded results?
followUps.answer: Retrieve per variant, union the chunks, dedupe by id, and optionally rerank the combined pool so the best across all variants rises to the top before generation.

followUps.question: What's the downside of expansion?
followUps.answer: Each variant is another retrieval (and possibly rerank) call adding latency and potential noise; you cap the number of variants and use it only where recall is the bottleneck.

scenario.question: Your chatbot's RAG works on first questions but fails on follow-ups like 'and does it support SSO?'. How do you redesign retrieval to fix this?
scenario.directAnswer: The follow-up embeds poorly because 'it' has no retrievable entity, so add a query-rewriting step that resolves references against chat history into a standalone search query before retrieval. If some questions are multi-hop, promote retrieval to a tool in an agentic loop so the model can search, read, and issue a follow-up query, bounded by a step cap. Route simple well-phrased queries down the cheap classic path and only conversational/multi-hop ones through rewriting and the agentic loop, and measure recall@k before and after to confirm the fix.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A conversational-retrieval failure caused by embedding under-specified follow-up queries verbatim.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Follow-ups rely on prior-turn context (pronouns, elided entities) that the retriever never sees, so the query vector lacks the terms needed to match relevant chunks.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Insert an LLM rewrite that produces a standalone query from history plus the latest message; retrieve on the rewrite; for compositional needs, loop retrieval as a tool with a termination bound; gate the extra machinery to the queries that need it and validate with retrieval metrics.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows fixing retrieval at the input (the cheapest, highest-leverage change) before reaching for heavier machinery, and gating cost to the queries that actually need it.
scenario.realWorldExample: Adding history-aware rewriting lifted recall@5 on follow-up turns from 0.4 to 0.85; only genuinely multi-hop questions were routed into the agentic loop to keep latency low.

followUps.question: How do you avoid rewriting harming already-good queries?
followUps.answer: Make the rewrite conservative (only resolve references / add missing entities) and A/B it on retrieval metrics; if a query is already standalone the rewrite should return it largely unchanged.

followUps.question: How do you keep the agentic loop from being slow?
followUps.answer: Cap steps, route only conversational/multi-hop queries into it, and let the agent skip retrieval entirely when it can answer from context.

keyTakeaways: Classic RAG retrieves once on the raw query; agentic RAG lets the agent rewrite, expand, and iterate — owning the retrieval strategy.
Rewriting resolves pronouns and adds keywords so conversational queries embed to something the index can match — often the biggest single retrieval win.
Expansion generates several sub-queries and merges results to raise recall, trading extra retrieval calls for broader coverage.
Making retrieval a tool the agent calls unlocks multi-step retrieval: search, read, and issue a follow-up query for compositional, multi-hop questions.
Let the agent decide when to retrieve (skip greetings/known facts) and always bound the loop with a step cap and an 'answer now' condition.
